title: Structural Insights into Brain-Penetrant EGFR Tyrosine Kinase Inhibitors with Enhanced Potency.
authors: Lantry AM, Weber TM, Damghani T et al.
abstract: An increasing focus on neurological diseases has led to a desire to enhance kinase inhibitor exposure within the central nervous system (CNS). In an effort to replicate their success in lung cancer, tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) targeting EGFR have been redesigned for enhanced blood-brain barrier (BBB) penetration, with several reaching clinical trials. To better understand the structural and functional attributes of these BBB-penetrating TKIs, we carried out X-ray crystallographic experiments and potency measurements. Our results show that structural alterations aimed at rationally enhancing CNS exposure result in diverse interactions with various regions of the EGFR kinase domains. Both biochemical and cellular potency are improved by these new moieties designed to enhance BBB penetration, with the most effective being those that introduce salt bridges with EGFR when combined with certain halogen substitutions. This work provides a rational framework for achieving a "two-for-one" benefit to drug profile, in which optimization of CNS exposure and target binding can be accomplished together.

title: Analysis of clinical and pathological characteristics of 10 cases of fetal lung adenocarcinoma.
authors: Qiu Y, Liu W, Jin Q et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Fetal adenocarcinoma of the lung (FLAC) is a rare subtype of lung adenocarcinoma resembling the developing fetal lung at the pseudoglandular stage (8-16 weeks of gestation). This study investigates the clinicopathological features, along with key diagnostic and treatment considerations for FLAC.
METHODS: Clinical data from 10 FLAC patients diagnosed at Linyi People's Hospital between January 2017 and December 2024 were retrospectively analyzed. Their clinicopathological characteristics were summarized in conjunction with relevant literature.
RESULTS: The cohort comprised low-grade FLAC (L-FLAC, 6 cases) and high-grade FLAC (H-FLAC, 4 cases). Pathological examinations indicated higher frequencies of pleural invasion (3/4) and lymph node metastasis (1/4) in H-FLAC, which exhibited marked nuclear atypia and abundant mitoses, while L-FLAC demonstrated mild cellular atypia and morular structures. Immunohistochemistry revealed universal positivity for TTF-1. Napsin A expression was noted in both L-FLAC (3/3) and H-FLAC (2/4). In L-FLAC, β-catenin showed nuclear/cytoplasmic or nuclear expression in the vast majority of cases while H-FLAC displayed only membranous expression. Molecular testing detected an EGFR exon 19 deletion in one H-FLAC case and a KRAS G12C mutation in another. No recurrence was observed during follow-up, which ranged from 4 to 93 months.
CONCLUSION: FLAC exhibits distinctive morphological features and immunophenotypes, necessitating differential diagnosis from primary pulmonary tumors and metastatic malignancies. Surgical resection remains the primary therapeutic strategy. No disease recurrence was observed during follow-up from 4 to 93 months, although some patients had a shorter follow-up period of 4-6 months.

title: Quality of Life Outcomes From the Phase 3 Study of Atezolizumab + Bevacizumab and Chemotherapy (ATTLAS, KCSG-LU19-04) in EGFR/ALK-Mutated Non-Small-Cell Lung Cancer.
authors: Kang EJ, Park S, Kim TM et al.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: The phase 3 ATTLAS study demonstrated that atezolizumab plus bevacizumab, carboplatin, and paclitaxel (ABCP) improved progression-free survival compared with pemetrexed-carboplatin/cisplatin (PC) in EGFR/ALK-mutated non-small-cell lung cancer after tyrosine kinase inhibitor failure. We report patient-reported quality of life (QoL) outcomes.
METHODS: Patients received ABCP (atezolizumab 1200 mg, bevacizumab 15 mg/kg, carboplatin AUC 5-5.5, paclitaxel 175 mg/m2) or PC (pemetrexed 500 mg/m2, carboplatin AUC 5.0, or cisplatin 70 mg/m2) every 3 weeks. QoL was assessed using EORTC QLQ-C30 and QLQ-LC13. Primary endpoints were changes in global health status/QoL (GHS/QoL) from baseline at weeks 9 and 24, and median time to deterioration (TTD; ≥ 10-point decline).
RESULTS: Of 228 randomized patients (2:1), 146 (ABCP) and 68 (PC) completed ≥ 1 QoL assessment. Baseline GHS/QoL was comparable between arms. Early GHS and physical functioning scores were numerically lower with ABCP but stabilized by week 24, with no significant differences at week 9 (-4.66; p = 0.247) or week 24 (-7.39; p = 0.305). Toxicity-related symptoms (neuropathy, alopecia, and pain) were more frequent with ABCP, whereas cancer-related symptom improvements (cough, dyspnea, and hemoptysis) occurred in both arms without significant differences. Median TTD was 3.48 months (ABCP) versus 6.90 months (PC; p = 0.160).
CONCLUSIONS: Despite impairment in symptoms commonly associated with chemotherapy, no significant between-group difference in overall QoL was detected between ABCP and PC. Stable GHS/QoL and improvement in cancer-related symptoms were observed alongside appropriate toxicity management.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: The protocol was approved by the institutional review board of Samsung Medical Center (IRB no. 2019-03-027) and participating centers (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT03991403).

title: [Clinical Challenges of Genetic Testing in Routine Practice and Proposals for Solutions-The Evolving Role of Companion Diagnostics].
authors: Kishikawa S, Yatabe Y
abstract: Companion diagnostics (CDx) and other molecular tests have been essential components of precision oncology, guiding treatment selection according to individual tumor profiles. In the 2000s, CDx largely followed a"one drug-one biomarker" model, in which single analyte assays for makers such as HER2, EGFR, and KRAS were paired with specific targeted therapies. With the rapid expansion of molecularly targeted agents and immune checkpoint inhibitors, this model has become increasingly limited. As a result, next-generation sequencing (NGS)-based multiplex CDx assays have been adopted to access multiple actionable alterations simultaneously. More recently, tumor-agnostic agents targeting NTRK fusions or MSI-H/ dMMR have further accelerated a shift toward organ- and drug-agnostic diagnostic platforms. In lung cancer, several multi-plex CDx and multi-gene tests-including the Lung Cancer Compact Panel, Oncomine Dx Target Test, AmoyDx, and MINtS are now widely used. Each has distinct advantages and limitations in terms of required sample volume, gene coverage, turnaround time, and cost. Therefore, test selection and its combination can be arranged according to clinical context and institutional resources. At the same time, practical challenges remain, including false-negative results due to suboptimal specimens or incomplete gene coverage, as well as delays in reporting and limitations in reimbursement. This article reviews the evolving role of companion diagnostics, the challenges and potential strategies for appropriately integrating these genetic tests into routine clinical practice, and future perspectives in this field.

title: Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor-Mutation Testing in Patients with Resected Stage IB-IIIB Lung Adenocarcinoma: Are Guidelines Followed?
authors: Pohlman A, Seder CW, Woodard GA et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Testing for Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor (EGFR)-mutations in resected stage IB-IIIB non-squamous non-small cell lung cancer is now standard for all patients, regardless of demographics. Current hospital- and patient-level testing rates and trends are unknown. In this context, we analyze hospital- and patient-level variation in EGFR testing nationally.
METHODS: We used the national cancer database (NCDB) to identify patients with stage IB-IIIB lung adenocarcinoma between 2021-2023 undergoing resection. We used a hierarchical multivariable logistic regression model to create risk- and reliability-adjusted EGFR testing rates across hospitals and compare those across quintiles. We also used a logistic regression model to compare the likelihood of testing based on patient demographics and socioeconomic factors.
RESULTS: Of 25,124 stage IB-IIIB patients with lung adenocarcinoma undergoing surgery, 14,061 (56.0%) patients at 906 hospitals were tested for EGFR mutations. There was significant variation in testing rates between hospitals (20.8% lowest quintile vs 89.7% highest, p<0.001). Hospitals were more likely to perform EGFR testing if they were academic centers (40.2% vs 38.6%, p=0.009) and reside in a metropolitan area (84.2% vs 81.8%, p<0.001). Patients were more likely to be tested if they were female (aOR 1.13, p<0.001), Asian (aOR 1.45, p<0.001), and never smokers (aOR 1.22, p<0.001).
CONCLUSIONS: Only 1 in 2 patients with stage IB-IIIB lung adenocarcinoma treated surgically are tested for EGFR mutations, with wide variation in care between hospitals and patients. Further quality initiatives are needed to target hospitals and providers and raise awareness to ensure guideline-concordant care.

title: Delayed Application of Immune Checkpoint Inhibitors in Advanced Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer
conditions: Metastatic NSCLC - Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer
summary: This study is a multicenter, randomized, open-label phase 3 trial of delayed administration of immunotherapy in patients who are planned to receive chemoimmunotherapy for newly diagnosed, advanced or metastatic, PD-L1 positive NSCLC without sensitizing alterations in EGFR, ALK, or ROS1.

title: A Phase II Study of Ivonescimab Combined With Iza-bren in Patients With Advanced Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer.
sponsor: Second Affiliated Hospital, Zhejiang University, School of Medicine
summary: This is a prospective, multicenter, open-label, single-arm phase II clinical study evaluating the efficacy and safety of ivonescimab (a PD-1/VEGF bispecific antibody) combined with Iza-bren (BL-B01D1; izalontamab brengitecan, an EGFR×HER3 bispecific antibody-drug conjugate) in patients aged ≥18 years with histologically or cytologically confirmed unresectable locally advanced (stage IIIB/IIIC) or metastatic (stage IV) non-squamous non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) harboring EGFR-sensitizing mutations (exon 19 deletion or L858R) who have imaging-confirmed disease progression during or after prior third-generation EGFR-TKI therapy. A total of 43 subjects will be enrolled at 3 centers. The primary endpoint is progression-free survival (PFS). Other efficacy endpoints include ORR, confirmed ORR, DCR, DoR, OS, 6- and 12-month PFS rates, and 12- and 24-month OS rates. Safety and tolerability will be assessed, and exploratory analyses will evaluate immune markers, HER3 expression, and EGFR resistance molecular subtypes in relation to clinical efficacy. Treatment is given every 3 weeks: ivonescimab 20 mg/kg intravenously on Day 1; Iza-bren 2.5 mg/kg intravenously on Days 1 and 8. Ivonescimab is infused first, followed by Iza-bren after an interval of ≥30 minutes. Treatment continues until disease progression, intolerable toxicity, initiation of new anti-cancer therapy, death, withdrawal of consent, or a maximum of 24 months of treatment.

title: A Study to Investigate the Efficacy and Safety of Dato-DXd-based Combinations in Participants With TROP2 NMR+ NSCLC
summary: Phase II, open-label, multicentre, multi-cohort platform study to determine the efficacy and safety of Datopotamab Deruxtecan (Dato-DXd)-based combinations for the treatment of TROP2 NMR+ NSCLC.

title: PET/CT Radiomics and Clinical Features for Classifying Transcriptome-Defined Immune Subgroups in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer: A Retrospective Study.
authors: Huang L, Dai Y, Su Y et al.
abstract: Tumor immune phenotypes are clinically relevant in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), but tissue-based assessment is invasive and vulnerable to sampling bias. This retrospective observational study evaluated whether positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) radiomic features combined with clinical variables could classify transcriptome-defined immune subgroups. Data from 184 patients were analyzed between January 2021 and December 2024 and used a computer-generated stratified 7:3 split to form a modeling cohort (n = 129) and an internal validation cohort (n = 55). Consensus clustering of transcriptomic profiles defined two immune subgroups. After reproducibility filtering, minimum redundancy maximum relevance analysis and least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) logistic regression retained six radiomic features. The final combined model included the radiomic score, smoking history, pathological type, and pleural adhesion. The combined model achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.841 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.772-0.909) in the modeling cohort and 0.822 (95% CI = 0.712-0.932) in the validation cohort. Compared with the radiomics-only model, the AUC gain was significant in the modeling cohort (p = 0.014) but not in the validation cohort (p = 0.590). At the modeling-derived threshold of 0.502, sensitivity and specificity were 76.5% and 82.0% in the modeling cohort and 75.9% and 69.2% in the validation cohort. Calibration intercepts and slopes were approximately 0 and 1.000 in the modeling cohort and -0.229 and 1.310 in the validation cohort. These findings support an internally evaluated association between routine PET/CT phenotypes and transcriptome-defined immune subgroups, but external validation and recalibration are required before clinical use.

title: Trilaciclib With Platinum-based Chemotherapy Followed by Avelumab Maintenance as First-line Treatment in Patients With Locally Advanced or Metastatic Urothelial Carcinoma: PRESERVE 3 Phase II Trial.
authors: Font A, Chkhotua A, Makharadze T et al.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Trilaciclib is a CDK4/6 inhibitor approved by the FDA to decrease the incidence of chemotherapy-induced myelosuppression in adults receiving chemotherapy for extensive-stage small cell lung cancer. This trial examined the antitumor efficacy and myeloprotection of trilaciclib with gemcitabine plus platinum-based chemotherapy followed by avelumab maintenance therapy for locally advanced/metastatic urothelial cancer (UC).
PATIENTS AND METHODS: In this open-label phase II trial, 92 patients randomized 1:1 received first-line platinum-based chemotherapy followed by avelumab maintenance therapy (control no trilaciclib) or plus trilaciclib. The primary endpoint was progression-free survival (PFS) during the overall trial period.
RESULTS: Median PFS was 6.6 months for trilaciclib versus 6.1 months for control in the overall study period (hazard ratio [HR] 0.94; 80% confidence interval [CI] 0.69-1.29; P = .885), and 3.8 months for trilaciclib versus 4.0 months for control in the maintenance period (HR 0.99; 80% CI 0.66-1.48; P = .577). In the cisplatin subgroup during the overall treatment period, 16.7% of trilaciclib patients versus 4.4% of control patients had a complete response, and 41.7% versus 47.8%, respectively, had an objective response. In cycle 1, severe (grade 4) neutropenia duration and incidence was 0.5 (SE 2.00) days and 6.7%/n = 3 for trilaciclib versus 0.8 (SE 2.88) days and 10.6%/n = 5 for control. Toxicity was manageable and consistent with previous trials.
CONCLUSIONS: Adding trilaciclib to platinum‑based chemotherapy followed by avelumab maintenance had modest myeloprotective effects and did not improve antitumor efficacy in patients with advanced UC, although the higher CR rate in combination with cisplatin-gemcitabine merits investigation. Early termination limits interpretation.

title: Molecular adequacy of image-guided biopsy techniques in non-small cell lung cancer: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
authors: Marinelli L, Brunese MC, Patanè V et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: In non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), image-guided biopsy must provide tissue for both diagnosis and biomarker-driven treatment selection. We systematically evaluated molecular adequacy of image-guided biopsy techniques for NSCLC biomarker profiling.
METHODS: PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, CENTRAL, and CDSR were searched from inception to 30 May 2026, supplemented by reference screening and forward citation tracking. Eligible studies reported extractable numerator-denominator data for molecular/genotyping adequacy, NGS/genotyping adequacy, PD-L1 adequacy, diagnostic yield, or procedure-related complications. Random-effects meta-analyses of logit-transformed proportions used restricted maximum-likelihood estimation, with I2, τ2, and 95% prediction intervals.
RESULTS: Twenty-six studies were included; 25 contributed to the main quantitative evidence base. The primary analysis included 23 study arms and yielded pooled molecular/genotyping adequacy of 89.5% (95% CI, 84.3-93.2%; I2 = 91.2%; τ2 = 1.070), with a 95% prediction interval of 48.4-98.7%. Pooled NGS/genotyping adequacy was 88.4% (95% CI, 80.9-93.1%; I2 = 91.6%), PD-L1 adequacy 93.9% (95% CI, 91.5-95.6%; I2 = 62.9%), and diagnostic yield 91.7% (95% CI, 86.3-95.1%). Sensitivity analyses did not materially alter the primary estimate.
CONCLUSIONS: Image-guided biopsy provides high average molecular and biomarker adequacy in NSCLC, but performance varies substantially across clinical, procedural, and laboratory settings. Pooled estimates should be interpreted within study-specific testing denominators and workflows rather than as unconditional probabilities of successful biomarker profiling. Diagnostic success and molecular readiness should be reported as distinct outcomes.

title: Alcohol use reduces the efficacy of anti-PD1 immunotherapy by disrupting antitumor immunity.
authors: Gilley KN, Garness J, Khan A et al.
abstract: Immune checkpoint inhibition (ICI) has improved outcomes for some patients with advanced malignancies, but relatively few have a complete response. Alcohol use is common and impairs adaptive immunity. Here, we explored the link between alcohol use and ICI efficacy in mouse models of lung and bladder cancers and performed a retrospective assessment of a cohort of patients with cancer receiving ICI therapy. In both mouse models, a regimen of moderate-to-heavy ethanol intake reduced ICI efficacy by ∼50% and increased tumor recurrence. In patients with lung cancer, regular alcohol use was associated with reduced survival benefit from ICI. Effects were less definitive in patients with bladder cancer, melanoma, and head and neck cancer, in whom alcohol use reporting was too limited. In mice bearing MB49 bladder tumors, ethanol intake reduced the number of tumor-infiltrated T cells favoring T helper 17 cell (TH17 cell) over TH1 cell phenotypes in tumor-associated CD4+ T cells. It also reduced the number of tissue-resident memory T cells, increased the proportion of T cells expressing the alternative immune checkpoint receptor TIGIT, and induced SREBP-mediated lipid signaling in tumor-associated T cells. Blocking TIGIT with antibodies or, to a lesser extent, inhibiting SREBP signaling with betulin improved the efficacy of PD1 receptor blockade. The findings suggest that regular alcohol use negatively affects ICI efficacy, which may be counteracted by cotargeting TIGIT. Future incorporation of patients' alcohol use in cancer databases will help define its effect on the outcome of various therapies in multiple cancers.

title: Midlife Cardiorespiratory Fitness and Site-Specific Cancer Outcomes in Men.
authors: Meernik C, Leonard D, Shuval K et al.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Higher cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF) is associated with a lower risk of cancer and mortality after diagnosis. However, mortality data are generally not specific to cancer sites or causes of death, limiting insights into the underlying mechanisms and opportunities for targeted prevention and survivorship strategies. This study aimed to examine the association between CRF and site-specific cancer incidence and mortality after diagnosis in men.
METHODS: This cohort study used data from the Cooper Center Longitudinal Study (1971-2018) linked to Medicare claims (1999-2019). CRF was estimated using a maximal treadmill test. The associations between CRF and site-specific cancer incidence and death after cancer for the leading cancer sites in men (colorectal, lung, and prostate) were estimated using multivariable illness-death models and proportional hazards regression with Gompertz baseline hazards.
RESULTS: Among 28,612 men with a mean Medicare follow-up of 7.9 years to cancer incidence, 4,998 colorectal, lung, and prostate cancers were identified. Higher CRF was associated with a lower risk of colorectal (HR: 0.91 per metabolic equivalent of task [MET]; 95% CI: 0.87, 0.96) and lung cancer (HR: 0.81 per MET; 95% CI: 0.77, 0.85), but not prostate cancer. During a mean follow-up of 7.1 years to death after diagnosis of colorectal, lung, or prostate cancer, 1,549 deaths were identified. High- (vs. low-) fit men with colorectal, lung, or prostate cancer had a 33-41% lower likelihood of all-cause mortality, including a generally lower risk of death from cardiovascular disease and other non-cancer causes.
CONCLUSIONS: Achieving higher CRF levels may contribute to cancer prevention and longer survival after diagnosis. Interventions that increase CRF through physical activity may improve health across the cancer control continuum.

title: Pulmonary rehabilitation in advanced non-small cell lung cancer receiving first-line immunotherapy: a multistakeholder analysis of barriers, willingness, and referral practices.
authors: Lekka C, Chynkiamis N, Zamarias V et al.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To assess barriers to pulmonary rehabilitation (PR), post-information willingness, subsequent participation, and physician referral practices among patients with advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) receiving first-line immunotherapy, using a multistakeholder approach.
METHODS: This observational study included 203 participants (83 patients, 60 caregivers, and 60 physicians) and combined cross-sectional stakeholder questionnaires with prospective follow-up of the patient cohort. Patients with stage IV NSCLC receiving first-line immune checkpoint inhibitor-based therapy who had initially declined PR completed questionnaires assessing barriers, perceptions, and willingness after structured information. Caregivers and physicians completed parallel questionnaires. Exploratory multivariable logistic regression examined factors associated with post-information willingness.
RESULTS: Lack of recommendation from the treating physician was the most frequently reported patient barrier (36/83, 43.4%), followed by fear of deterioration and fatigue. After structured information, 68/83 patients (81.9%) were willing to participate; 35/68 (51.5%) subsequently initiated PR and 28/35 (80.0%) completed the program. Positive baseline PR perception was associated with greater post-information willingness after adjustment for age and treating-physician recommendation (adjusted OR 9.23, 95% CI 1.79-47.57; p=.008). High patient willingness, caregiver support, and physician awareness coexisted with lower self-reported physician referral rates.
CONCLUSION: Among initial PR decliners with advanced NSCLC receiving first-line ICI-based therapy, lack of treating-physician recommendation was the most common barrier. High post-information willingness contrasted with lower subsequent participation, supporting further prospective study of factors influencing PR referral and participation.

title: Febuxostat inhibits non-small cell lung cancer cell proliferation under starvation conditions by modulating xanthine oxidoreductase-associated autophagy.
authors: Yao XH, Shao M, Xu YW
abstract: Febuxostat (FBX), a selective non-purine xanthine oxidoreductase (XOR) inhibitor clinically indicated for hyperuricemia, has recently attracted attention for its potential antitumor properties. Nevertheless, its potential therapeutic efficacy against non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) remains to be fully characterized. XOR expression and enzymatic activity were quantified in NSCLC lines (A549 and SK-MES-1) and compared with normal human bronchial epithelial BEAS-2B cells. The effects of XOR and FBX on cell proliferation, migration and invasion were evaluated using the cell counting kit-8, wound-healing and Matrigel-Transwell invasion assays, respectively. Apoptosis and autophagic flux under starvation conditions (FBS-free DMEM) were assessed using Annexin V/SYTOX staining, DCFH-DA, western blotting (p62 and LC3-II) and LysoTracker Red staining. The functional role of autophagy was validated through rescue experiments using the autophagy activator rapamycin. XOR was found to be markedly upregulated and hyperactive in NSCLC cells compared with normal epithelial cells. Small interfering RNA-mediated XOR knockdown attenuated NSCLC cell viability, migration and invasion. Pharmacological inhibition of XOR by FBX likewise impaired proliferative, migratory and invasive capacities, accompanied by marked suppression of autophagic flux. Notably, these antitumor effects were abrogated by rapamycin-induced autophagy activation. The present findings demonstrated that XOR is involved in the metabolic drive of NSCLC progression under nutrient-deprived conditions. Specifically, FBX exerted anticancer effects by blocking XOR-mediated pathways and suppressing protective autophagy, suggesting that repurposing FBX for NSCLC therapy warrants further preclinical investigation.

title: Dual-target CAR-T cells in triple-negative breast cancer: recent advances and translational challenges.
authors: Su J, Wang B, Xiao H et al.
abstract: Treatment options for triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) remain extremely limited, and patients have a poor prognosis. Although chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapy has achieved breakthroughs in haematological malignancies, its application in solid tumours such as TNBC is hampered by challenges including antigenic heterogeneity, immune evasion, and off-target toxicity. By simultaneously targeting two tumour-associated antigens, dual-target CAR-T cell therapy may broaden antigen coverage and reduce the likelihood of antigen-negative tumour escape in preclinical models; however, their clinical efficacy and safety in TNBC remain unestablished. This study summarises the structural characteristics and functional differences among the three mainstream engineering strategies for dual-target CAR-T cell therapy, with a particular focus on the current evidence from preclinical studies in TNBC regarding target combinations such as B7-H3/CSPG4, MSLN/NKG2DLs and TROP2/B7-H3. At the same time, this paper highlights that dual-target CAR-T cell therapy for TNBC still faces key bottlenecks, including uncertainty in target selection, a narrow safety margin, immunosuppression within the tumour microenvironment, and a lack of clinical evidence. Future research should focus on establishing high-quality antigen expression profiles, optimising CAR structural design, and exploring combinatorial strategies with microenvironment-modulating agents to advance the translation of dual-target CAR-T cell therapy clinical translation of for TNBC.

title: Continuous in situ production of CAR T cells from in vivo-transduced HSCs is safe and delays growth of mouse HER2high tumors.
authors: Li C, Wang H, Long AY et al.
abstract: Clinical trials with CAR T cells for solid tumors have suggested a number of problems, including critical autoimmune reactions caused by high-affinity CAR T cells, development of CAR T cell exhaustion, poor trafficking to tumor sites after intravenous CAR T cell injection, and high costs. To address these problems, we tested an in vivo HSC gene therapy approach, resulting in in situ production of low-affinity mHER2-CAR-expressing T-cells in physiologically relevant immunocompetent mouse models with tumors derived from mouse HER2high tumor cell lines, KPmHER2 and B16F10mHER2. After intravenous injection of integrating helper-dependent adenovirus (HDAd) vectors expressing mHER2-CAR under T cell restricted transcriptional and miRNA control into mobilized C57BL/6-based mice and in vivo enrichment of stably transduced HSCs, we demonstrated that mHER2-CAR T cells significantly delayed tumor growth. Additional Treg depletion by systemic administration of low-dose cyclophosphamide further extended the time of tumor relapse driven by mHER2-negative cells. Despite continuous mHER2-CAR T cell production, the in vivo approach had an excellent safety profile. Our study also revealed a number of obstacles that limit the efficacy of the in vivo approach and have to be addressed in the future.

title: Nanomedicine-Enabled in vivo CAR-Macrophage Engineering: Human Evidence, Translational Bottlenecks, and a Validation Framework.
authors: He H, Sun J, Xu J et al.
abstract: Nanomedicine is enabling in vivo chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) engineering of myeloid cells, but exposure and uptake do not establish a functional CAR-macrophage product. This oncology-focused narrative review organizes the evidence along five stages: anatomical access, cellular uptake, productive intracellular availability, CAR-protein expression, and antigen-dependent function. Cell identity and state are a cross-stage validation dimension rather than a sixth sequential event. Human tumor-associated macrophage atlases motivate measuring which cells express CAR, while an all-human acute myeloid leukemia screen challenges a universal CD47-centered phagocytosis hierarchy. Neither establishes a universally preferred solid-tumor macrophage state or checkpoint. We distinguish murine and human preclinical studies, peer-reviewed patient data, conference reports, sponsor disclosures, and trial registrations. Early in vivo myeloid programs support technical feasibility and repeat dosing, whereas clinically meaningful efficacy and state-selective engineering remain insufficiently established in the selected evidence. Protein-first assays, endpoint-matched models, quantitative cellular pharmacology, and product-specific potency testing offer a practical validation framework, with no validated universal thresholds. The literature cutoff is 31 August 2026. Clinical web information was checked through 12 August 2026.

title: Anti-PD-L1 antibody limits the survival of activated CAR T cells by disrupting the PD-L1/CD80 cis-heterodimer.
authors: Li SS, Barden M, Pan H et al.
abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells have revolutionized the treatment of hematologic malignancies but remain less efficacious in solid tumors. While PD-L1 blockade is widely used to counter tumor immune evasion, its direct effects on activated T cells, which also express PD-L1 and may engage in PD-L1/CD80 cis-interactions, remain largely unexplored. To investigate this, we blocked PD-L1 by engineering CAR T cells that secrete PD-L1-blocking single-chain variable fragment (scFv) antibodies derived from atezolizumab. Secretion of the scFv conferred no benefit: 4-1BB-based CAR T cells accumulated less upon repeated antigen stimulation, and CD28-based CAR T cells killed less efficiently when effector cells were limiting. Mechanistically, PD-L1 and CD80 form a cis-heterodimer on T cells that is disrupted by PD-L1 blockade, rendering CD80 susceptible to CTLA-4-mediated depletion and impairing CD28 co-stimulation. Consistent with this model, exogenous atezolizumab reduced CD80 expression and T cell viability, while CTLA-4 blockade with ipilimumab restored CD80 levels and rescued survival. These findings were corroborated by structural modeling demonstrating that atezolizumab disrupts the PD-L1/CD80 complex, and were reproduced in unmodified T cells and across both CD28- and 4-1BB-based CARs. Together, our findings uncover a T cell-intrinsic vulnerability to PD-L1 inhibitors that warrants consideration when PD-L1 blockade is combined with adoptive T cell therapy.

title: Genetically engineered extracellular vesicles with chimeric antigen receptors of human stem cell-derived neutrophils targeting fibroblast activation protein to modulate tumor microenvironment.
authors: Esmonde C, Sun L, Jin G et al.
abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most commonly occurring central nervous system tumor, accounting for over 50% of gliomas, with a poor survival rate. A primary driver of GBM progression is the fibrotic stroma, where excess extracellular matrix deposition creates a dense network that excludes immune cells and chemotherapeutic agents. While targeting tumor-associated fibroblasts (TAFs) via fibroblast activation protein (FAP)-directed chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) immune cells is a promising strategy, off-target toxicities limit the clinical utility of the treatment. To address these safety concerns, extracellular vesicles (EVs) of FAP-CAR-engineered neutrophils differentiated from human pluripotent stem cells were isolated and characterized, including proteomic profile, microRNA content, in vitro bioactivity, and in vivo biodistribution in this study. Multi-omic profiling revealed that CAR engineering enriched EVs with proinflammatory proteins, iron-transferring proteins, and proliferation regulators, and a significant upregulation of miRNAs targeting FAP and proliferation-regulating genes was observed. Functional in vitro assays demonstrated that these EVs are selectively cytotoxic to TAFs, reducing the expression of BCL-2 and RAS-MAPK-ERK signaling pathway genes. These EVs also demonstrated cytotoxicity to patient-derived GBM spheroids. Furthermore, in vivo biodistribution results confirmed that FAP-CAR EVs are capable of systemic circulation and payload delivery, showing a significant increase in accumulation within the liver and spleen compared to free Cy5.5. These findings suggest that CAR engineering enhances the ability of FAP-CAR EVs to inhibit TAF proliferation and induce apoptosis. FAP-targeting CAR EVs are positioned as a targeted bioengineered delivery platform with the potential for remodeling the tumor microenvironment and slowing the progression of desmoplasia in GBM.

title: A CD7-targeted AAV variant enables efficient T and NK cell engineering in vivo.
authors: Hong L, Chen G, Liu Y et al.
abstract: Adeno-associated virus (AAV) vectors have been applied for precise genome engineering in human T cells but poor tropism restricts their efficiency and translational potential. Here, through directed evolution of the AAV6 capsid in primary human T cells, we identified a family of variants containing an APR motif at residues 455-457. The lead candidate, AAV.APR31, enabled robust transduction of primary T and NK cells at nearly 100-1,000-fold lower doses than AAV6 and outperformed the human T cell-tropic capsid AAV-hT7. CRISPR screening identified CD7 as a lineage-specific entry enhancer alongside the canonical AAVR pathway and structural analysis suggested that the APR motif facilitates CD7 engagement. Unlike existing delivery systems confined to one engineering mode, AAV.APR31 enabled transient transgene delivery, site-specific knock-in and transposon integration in human T and NK cells, generating CAR-T cells functionally equivalent to lentiviral vector-manufactured products. Systemic administration of AAV.APR31-generated CAR-T cells in vivo resulted in potent tumor control in hematologic and solid tumor mouse models.

title: Gamma-delta T cells in neuroblastoma: Exploiting MHC-independent recognition to overcome the barriers of high-risk disease.
authors: Mohamadian S, Kalantari A, Farajifard H et al.
abstract: Neuroblastoma is the most frequent extracranial solid tumor in children and the main cause of early childhood cancer deaths. Relapse occurs in more than half of high-risk patients despite rigorous multimodal therapy, and four-year overall survival in relapsed disease is approximately 20%. Anti-GD2 monoclonal antibodies and GD2-directed CAR T cell treatment have advanced the field, although neither has eliminated neuroblastoma's immune resistance. Current immunotherapy has three interrelated challenges. GD2 heterogeneity lets antigen-negative subclones escape and cause recurrence. Inhibitory cytokines, regulatory T cells, and myeloid-derived suppressor cells dominate the TME. MHC class I downregulation frequently renders traditional αβ T cell methods ineffective, even with the target antigen present. Gamma-delta (γδ) T cells offer a distinct mechanism. They recognize tumor targets without antigen presentation by sensing stress-induced ligands through NKG2D and DNAM-1 and phosphoantigens through butyrophilin proteins BTN3A1 and BTN2A1. This recognition holds regardless of MHC class I status. In conjunction with anti-GD2 antibodies, CD16 expression boosts antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity. In neuroblastoma lesions, γδ T cells are the primary antitumoral fraction in tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte products, indicating compatibility with the disease's immune system. This study examines neuroblastoma immunotherapy failure mechanisms and innovative γδ T cell platforms, such as non-engineered allogeneic products, composite γδ T plus NK cell techniques, and CAR- and AbTCR-modified designs. A biomarker-driven patient selection paradigm and product standardization, in vivo persistence, and TME suppression are examined. NCT05400603, the first trial of adoptive transfer of ex vivo-expanded allogeneic γδ T cells in a population that includes pediatric neuroblastoma patients, is crucial for proving the mechanism.

title: Updated outcome of patients with lung only osteosarcoma recurrence following surgical resection enrolled in phase 2 clinical trials: A report from the Children's Oncology Group
summary: Objective: Osteosarcoma is a rare primary bone cancer of adolescents and young adults without significant improvement in treatments or outcomes in several decades. Resection is standard of care for recurrent disease. Patients with lung only osteosarcoma recurrence following surgical resection (LOOR-FSR) may present the most meaningful opportunity for impactful intervention but alternative trial endpoints to objective response are needed. Here we update benchmarks for LOOR-FSR with contemporary clinical trial data. Patients/Methods: This study included patients with pathologically confirmed LOOR-FSR enrolled on three Childrens Oncology Group phase 2 single arm trials. Benchmark endpoints assessed in this patient population were event-free survival (EFS) and overall survival (OS). In addition, we evaluated the impact of demographics and baseline clinical factors on outcome. Results: Ninety-nine patients met criteria for inclusion in this analysis. Median EFS and OS were 4.8 (95% CI: 3.5, 6.3) and 26.2 (23.3, 56.8) months respectively. Twelve-month EFS was 22% (15-31%) and ranged from 14% to 29% across the 3 trials, a difference that did not achieve statistical significance. The risk of EFS event was higher for those whose first recurrence occurred within two years of diagnosis (p=0.009). Other demographic and clinical factors did not statistically impact risk of event though estimated EFS for males was lower than for females. Conclusion: Despite almost doubling the number of patients in this historical control cohort, wide variance in outcomes led to confidence intervals unchanged from previously published work. Until the most significant factors contributing to variability of outcomes in this patient population are quantified, single arm trials of new approaches will only be able to identify large effect sizes. Smaller effect sizes will require randomization.

title: Integrated Genomic and Transcriptomic Profiling Reveals Distinct Biological Programs and Therapeutic Opportunities in Cancer of Unknown Primary
summary: Background: Cancer of unknown primary (CUP) is a metastatic, heterogeneous malignancy accounting for 2-5% of cancer diagnoses globally. Failure to identify the primary site precludes tumor-type-specific therapy and, together with an aggressive clinical course, contributes to poor survival. The biological mechanisms driving these behaviors remain poorly understood. A deeper understanding of CUP biology is therefore essential to improve diagnostic precision and therapeutic strategies. To address this knowledge gap, we comprehensively characterized the multi-omics landscape of CUP and identified biological and potentially therapeutic targets beyond tissue-of-origin (ToO) assignment. Methods: Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) data from 283 CUP patients were analyzed for ToO predictions, mutational signatures, driver alterations, genetic immune escape (GIE), and clinically actionable alterations. Matched RNA-sequencing (RNA-seq) data from 79 cases were used to characterize functional gene expression signatures and define transcriptomic subtypes. Clinical, WGS, and RNA-seq data were integrated via weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA). Results: High-confidence ToO predictions (likelihood >80%) were obtained for 58% of CUPs, most commonly predicting lung, gastrointestinal, and biliary tract origins. Mutational signatures clustering revealed four subgroups dominated by tobacco smoking, defective DNA mismatch repair (dMMR), UV exposure, and APOBEC activity, while a fifth group, comprising most tumors (n=169; 60%), showed mixed mutational processes. The cohort also frequently exhibited mutations in established cancer driver genes, including TP53, CDKN2A, KRAS, and epigenetic modifiers ARID1A, SMARCA4, and ARID2. GIE alterations occurred in 35% of tumors, mostly involving HLA-I genes. Transcriptomic profiling defined five subtypes with different degrees of immune infiltration, fibrosis, and tumor proliferation. These subtypes were not significantly associated with c

title: FasL blockade suppresses liver metastasis and prolongs survival in small-cell lung cancer
summary: Small-cell lung cancer (SCLC) is an aggressive malignancy characterised by early metastatic dissemination, frequent relapse and poor long-term survival. Despite advances in immunotherapy, durable disease control remains challenging, highlighting the need to identify therapeutic vulnerabilities beyond conventional tumour-cell killing and immune checkpoint inhibition. Here, we uncover an unexpected contribution of Fas-Fas ligand (FasL) signalling to SCLC metastatic progression and demonstrate the therapeutic potential of targeting this pathway. Using an autochthonous Rb1/Trp53-deficient mouse model, we show that genetic Fas deletion markedly suppresses liver metastatic disease, identifying a previously unrecognised contribution of Fas signalling to metastatic progression. Notably, despite this antimetastatic effect, Fas deletion during tumour initiation did not improve survival and was accompanied by pronounced alterations in pulmonary tissue architecture. As these alterations may reflect adverse consequences of Fas deletion in non-malignant pulmonary populations, we reasoned that pharmacological FasL blockade in established disease could provide therapeutic benefit while circumventing the detrimental consequences for pulmonary tissue homeostasis associated with genetic Fas deletion. Remarkably, only six administrations of a soluble Fas-Fc fusion protein over three weeks significantly prolonged survival and substantially reduced the incidence and burden of liver metastases. FasL blockade was also associated with enhanced inflammatory and immune-response transcriptional signatures in the liver, while its combination with anti-PD-1 increased pulmonary immune-cell accumulation without conferring additional survival benefit. These data suggest that the biological consequences of targeting this pathway may depend on the timing and cellular context of intervention. Together, our findings identify Fas-FasL signalling as an unexpected regulator of SCLC metastatic progression

title: Lorlatinib-associated sensorineural deafness in a non-small cell lung cancer patient with ALK-fusion: a Case Report.
authors: Cai L, Peng W, Yang R et al.
abstract: In the era of precision targeted therapy, anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK) tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) have significantly improved survival outcomes for patients with ALK-positive non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). The third-generation ALK inhibitor lorlatinib, characterized by superior antitumor activity, a broader spectrum of ALK mutation sites and enhanced central nervous system (CNS) penetrability, has yielded breakthrough clinical benefits. However, lorlatinib has a distinct adverse event profile, with edema, dyslipidemia, central and peripheral nervous system toxicities, posing key clinical management challenges. Herein, we report the first case of an ALK-fusion NSCLC patient who developed peripheral neuropathy, dysarthria, and sensorineural deafness following lorlatinib treatment. While dysarthria and peripheral neuropathy have been previously documented, sensorineural deafness is extremely rare, and no prior reports describe the concurrent and persistent onset of all three symptoms, underscoring the need for enhanced toxicity monitoring and patient education.

title: Daraxonrasib: First Approval.
authors: Syed YY
abstract: Daraxonrasib (RASONQUE™) is an oral, multiselective, noncovalent RAS(ON) inhibitor being developed by Revolution Medicines for the treatment of solid tumours, including pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), non-small-cell lung cancer and colorectal cancer. Daraxonrasib received its first approval in the USA on 26 August 2026 for the treatment of adults with metastatic PDAC who have received at least one prior systemic therapy or who are not candidates for multiagent systemic therapy. This article summarizes the milestones in the development of daraxonrasib leading to its first approval for metastatic PDAC.

title: Brigatinib plus carboplatin-pemetrexed after lorlatinib failure in ALK-rearranged non-small cell lung cancer with co-occurring ALK I1171N and G1269A mutations: a case report.
authors: Akagündüz F, Demir TH, Tunc MA et al.
abstract: No standard targeted strategy exists after lorlatinib failure in ALK-rearranged non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). We report a 41-year-old man with metastatic ALK-rearranged lung adenocarcinoma who progressed sequentially on alectinib and lorlatinib. Re-biopsy with DNA/RNA next-generation sequencing (NGS) at lorlatinib progression revealed an EML4::ALK fusion with co-occurring ALK I1171N and G1269A mutations at high allele fractions, suggesting a cis configuration. Supported by in vitro data, he received brigatinib plus carboplatin-pemetrexed. After four cycles, the primary tumor regressed markedly, nodal disease showed a complete metabolic response, and intracranial findings remained stable. Grade 2 fatigue was the only adverse event; maintenance pemetrexed plus brigatinib is ongoing. Concurrent chemotherapy and short follow-up preclude attributing the response to brigatinib alone. This case highlights the value of repeat biopsy and NGS after lorlatinib failure and suggests that a brigatinib-containing chemotherapy regimen is feasible in this setting.

title: Clinically Presumed Brain Metastasis as the Initial Presentation of Prostate Cancer Harboring a BRCA2 Alteration With Subsequent Transformation to Treatment-Related Neuroendocrine Prostate Cancer: A Case Report.
authors: Wang Y, Wu Y, Zhu S et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Treatment-related neuroendocrine prostate cancer (t-NEPC) is an aggressive, therapy-resistant phenotype for which no standard treatment has been established. Intracranial metastasis from prostate cancer is uncommon, particularly as the initial presentation.
CASE: In March 2020, a 62-year-old man presented to Nanfang Hospital, Southern Medical University, Guangzhou, China, with dizziness and blurred vision. Imaging showed disseminated prostate cancer and an intracranial lesion that was clinically presumed to represent metastasis but was not biopsied. Prostate biopsy demonstrated acinar adenocarcinoma (Gleason score 5 + 4 = 9; Grade Group 5). After androgen deprivation therapy, docetaxel, and subsequent abiraterone, a February 2022 transurethral resection specimen showed large-cell neuroendocrine carcinoma, establishing t-NEPC in the prostate. Immediately before TURP, total PSA was 0.369 ng/mL and NSE was 30.3 ng/mL. Tumor-only next-generation sequencing of the resection specimen detected BRCA2 p.I605fs and TP53 p.A83fs alterations with RB1 and PTEN copy-number losses; germline status was not assessed. Etoposide/cisplatin was initiated in March 2022, and continuous olaparib began on April 14, 2022 during cycle 2. Clinical improvement and approximately 11 months of disease stability were observed, but the contribution of either treatment cannot be isolated. The disease subsequently progressed, and the patient died 39 months after the initial diagnosis.
CONCLUSION: This case underscores the distinction between a clinically presumed intracranial metastasis and histologically confirmed t-NEPC. It also highlights the diagnostic value of re-biopsy at progression and the need for cautious interpretation of biomarker changes and overlapping treatments. Prospective clinicopathological and molecular data are needed to refine the diagnosis and management of t-NEPC.

title: [A Case of Chronic Encapsulated Expanding Hematoma Following Gamma Knife Radiosurgery for a Brain Metastasis from Large-Cell Neuroendocrine Carcinoma of the Lung].
authors: Ohno K, Sakaguchi K, Yomo S et al.
abstract: A 69-year-old man with large-cell neuroendocrine carcinoma of the left lung accompanied by brain and rectal metastases underwent Gamma knife radiosurgery followed by chemotherapy with atezolizumab, etoposide, and carboplatin, achieving a complete response. During maintenance therapy, enlargement of the treated brain lesion caused right lower extremity paresis; therefore, repeat Gamma knife radiosurgery was performed. Three years later, the recurrent paresis recurred. Contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging revealed a well-circumscribed lesion with a thick capsule in the left parietal lobe. Fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography/magnetic resonance imaging showed no abnormal uptake. Recurrent brain metastasis and chronic encapsulated expanding hematoma were considered in the differential diagnosis. A craniotomy and lesion resection were performed. Histopathological examination demonstrated an organized hematoma without viable malignant cells, leading to the diagnosis of chronic encapsulated expanding hematoma. The neurological deficit improved postoperatively. Chronic encapsulated expanding hematoma should therefore be considered in the differential diagnosis of recurrent brain metastasis after stereotactic radiosurgery.

title: PIK-75 suppresses SREBP-dependent sterol-synthesis genes in PIK3CA-altered small-cell lung cancer cells, but attribution to p110α remains unresolved.
authors: Movaqar A, Yaghoubi A, Rezaee SA
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Class IA PI3K isoforms are candidate therapeutic targets in small-cell lung cancer (SCLC). The transcriptional consequences of isoform-directed inhibitors in SCLC cells have not been compared genome-wide.
METHODS: We re-analysed GEO series GSE40564, in which PIK3CA-altered NCI-H69 cells were treated for 24 h with vehicle, PIK-75 (p110α-directed) or TGX-221 (p110β-directed), with three arrays per group. Differential expression used limma, with re-processing from raw files and spike-in-anchored normalisation as sensitivity analyses. Gene sets were tested with correlation-adjusted competitive tests (camera), including a direct comparison of the two compounds. The main finding was checked against LINCS L1000 signatures of selective PI3K inhibitors and an independent alpelisib RNA-seq dataset. Isoform dependency was examined in DepMap CRISPR screens, and a PIK-75 response score was tested in 81 primary SCLCs against matched random-signature nulls.
RESULTS: PIK-75 changed 11,645 of 17,458 genes at FDR < 0.05; 316 decreased and 20 increased significantly beyond two-fold. Its clearest pathway-level effect was lower expression of SREBP-controlled sterol- and lipid-synthesis genes (SQLE, HMGCS1, HMGCR, LDLR, SCD; log2 fold-change -1.1 to -1.6). Cholesterol homeostasis was the only gene set that stayed significant after correlation adjustment (camera FDR = 0.02) and that differed significantly between PIK-75 and TGX-221 (FDR = 0.02). TGX-221 changed 358 genes, none two-fold, and its response depended on two of three replicates. In LINCS, the down-regulated genes of alpelisib and taselisib were enriched for SREBP targets (p ≈ 5 × 10⁻⁶), whereas those of TGX-221 were not, and alpelisib reduced several of the same genes in an independent dataset. PIK-75 also inhibits CDK9 and DNA-PK, and canonical FOXO targets were not induced, so the response cannot be attributed to p110α alone. SCLC lines depended more on PIK3CA than on PIK3CB in DepMap (median Chronos -0.38 vs -0.15), as did other lineages. In patients, the response score was not associated with survival beyond matched random signatures (empirical p = 0.12-0.14).
CONCLUSION: To our knowledge, this is the first genome-wide comparison of isoform-directed PI3K inhibitors in SCLC cells. PIK-75, but not TGX-221, suppresses an SREBP-dependent sterol programme in NCI-H69 cells, and public data from selective p110α inhibitors point to PI3K signalling as its most plausible source. Because PIK-75 is not selective and TGX-221 exposure was not measured, the attribution to p110α and the apparent dispensability of p110β remain preliminary.

title: Pathway-specific conditional prognosis after definitive local therapy in stage III non-small cell lung cancer: a single-center retrospective landmark cohort study.
authors: Xu Z, Chang W, Jian M et al.
abstract:
AIMS: To describe conditional prognosis after redirection from neoadjuvant immunochemotherapy to definitive radiotherapy in stage III non-small cell lung cancer.
PATIENTS AND METHODS: This single-center retrospective study estimated noncausal prognosis in 116 selected patients alive and progression-free 42 days after local treatment: neoadjuvant immunochemotherapy followed by redirected definitive thoracic radiotherapy (NICT-dCRT; n = 36; concurrent chemotherapy in 35), definitive concurrent chemoradiotherapy with consolidation immunotherapy (CRT-CI; n = 43), or surgery after neoadjuvant immunochemotherapy (NICT-S; n = 37). Progression-free survival (PFS) was primary; overall survival (OS) was secondary. Kaplan-Meier and restricted mean survival time (RMST) summaries were emphasized; Firth Cox associations were secondary and exploratory. Overlap weighting failed to achieve adequate balance.
RESULTS: In NICT-dCRT and CRT-CI, median OS was 36.5 and 34.0 months, and median PFS was 17.1 and 13.4 months. Corresponding 24-month OS RMST was 20.59 and 20.86 months; PFS RMST was 16.63 and 15.24 months. Between-pathway RMST differences were imprecise. NICT-S had five PFS events and two deaths.
CONCLUSIONS: These estimates describe pathway-specific conditional prognosis in clinically distinct post-landmark populations. Clinical selection, sparse events, and residual confounding preclude treatment-superiority or equivalence claims.

title: T-cell engagers in solid tumors: challenges and emerging strategies.
authors: Forero J, Jani R, Zheng X et al.
abstract: T-cell engagers (TCEs) redirect endogenous T cells toward malignant cells by simultaneously binding a tumor-associated target and a T-cell receptor component, most commonly CD3, thereby inducing immune-synapse formation and cytotoxicity independently of conventional antigen recognition. Although TCEs have transformed the treatment of several hematologic malignancies, their development in solid tumors remain limited by heterogeneous and non-tumor-specific antigen expression, impaired tumor penetration and T-cell trafficking, an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, and immune-mediated toxicities. This review examines the structural and mechanistic foundations of TCE activity, including antibody fragment-based constructs, IgG-like bispecific antibodies, T-cell receptor-based engagers, and emerging multispecific platforms. We discuss how molecular size, valency, geometry, epitope location, binding affinity, and pharmacokinetic engineering influence immune-synapse quality, antitumor potency, cytokine release, tissue distribution. Major barrier efficacy, including on-target, off-tumor toxicity, antigen heterogeneity and escape, restricted T-cell infiltration, T-cell exhaustion, and metabolic and immunologic suppression are critically evaluated. The evolving clinical landscape across major solid tumors is reviewed, with emphasis on tebentafusp in metastatic uveal melanoma and tarlatamab in previously treated small-cell lung cancer, illustrating the importance of aligning target biology, molecular format, and dosing strategy. We also address cytokine release syndrome, neurologic toxicity, resistance, and treatment failure and highlight strategies designed to widen the therapeutic window and sustain antitumor activity, including step-up dosing, affinity and avidity tuning, conditional or protease-activated constructs, dual-target and trispecific platforms, localized or genetically encoded delivery, rational combinations, and predictive biomarkers. Together, these advances are positioning TCEs as an increasingly adaptable and durable therapeutic platform for solid tumors.

title: Sex, Smoking Status, and Long-Term Outcomes After Lung Cancer Resection: An STS General Thoracic Surgery Database Analysis.
authors: Alzghari T, Sewell M, Bonnell LN et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The incidence of lung cancer in women is increasing, yet the effect of smoking history on survival remains uncertain.
METHODS: Adults who underwent resection for non-small cell lung cancer (2015-2024), from the Society of Thoracic Surgeons database, were grouped by sex and smoking status. Outcomes were analyzed using multivariable logistic regression and Cox models.
RESULTS: In total, 145,103 patients were identified (current or former smoker women: 65,650 [45.2%]; current or former smoker men: 55,912 [38.5%]; never-smoker women: 16,902 [11.7%]; never-smoker men: 6,639 [4.6%]. Median age was 69 years. Never-smoker women were more likely to be Asian, have clinical stage I disease, and have adenocarcinoma; they also had the lowest rates of 30-day mortality and major morbidity. Current or former smoker men had the highest complications rates. These findings persisted after risk adjustment. Longitudinal mortality data were available for 59,756 patients (57%). Five-year survival was 79% for never-smoker women, 70% for never-smoker men, 71% for current or former smoker women, and 58% for current or former smoker men. Risk-adjusted survival was longer in women versus men and in never-smokers versus current or former smokers for both sexes. Compared with never-smoker women, all-cause mortality risk was higher in current or former smoker women (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR]=1.18 [95% confidence interval {CI},1.11-1.26]), never-smoker men (aHR=1.44[95% CI,1.30-1.60]), and current or former smoker men (aHR=1.71 [95% CI,1.59-1.84]).
CONCLUSIONS: Never-smoker women had the lowest perioperative risk and superior long-term survival, highlighting sex and smoking status as independent determinants of outcomes after lung cancer resection.

title: Longitudinal Detection of Circulating Tumor DNA in Children with Pleuropulmonary Blastoma: A Report from the International PPB/DICER1 Registry.
authors: Schultz KAP, Field AL, Mallinger PHR et al.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Pleuropulmonary blastoma (PPB) is the most common lung cancer of early childhood. Nearly all PPBs have biallelic DICER1 variants: a loss-of-function allele (often germline) and a second RNase IIIb domain "hotspot" substitution. Except in somatic mosaicism, these hotspots are tumor-specific and ideal liquid biopsy targets.
EXPERIMENTAL DESIGN: For individuals with PPB enrolled in the International PPB/DICER1 Registry, blood samples were collected at timepoints coordinated with clinical venous access. Tumor sequencing identified each patient's RNase IIIb hotspot, enabling personalized droplet digital PCR assays to detect that variant in circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA).
RESULTS: We analyzed 482 samples from 20 type I and 53 type II/III PPB patients. Among 13 pre-operative type II/III patients sampled pretreatment, 11 (85%) had detectable ctDNA, with tumor size moderately correlated with ctDNA burden (Spearman's ρ=0.574, p=0.051). In contrast, among 8 patients sampled after resection but before chemotherapy, none had detectable ctDNA (p<0.001 vs. unresected). After chemotherapy initiation, ctDNA levels spiked within 1-2 days before rapidly declining. During post-event surveillance, ctDNA was detectable a median of 5.3 weeks before clinical progression (21.7 weeks for negative samples; p=0.001). In type I PPB, DICER1 variants were detectable only in patients with somatic mosaicism.
CONCLUSIONS: In type II/III PPB, ctDNA correlates with tumor size and resection status. The transient rise and fall in ctDNA following initiation of chemotherapy suggests that ctDNA could serve as a real-time in vivo assay of tumor responsiveness, and these findings support further investigation as a pharmacodynamic biomarker for disease response and recurrence detection.

title: Corrigendum: Current status and future perspectives of liquid biopsy in non-small cell lung cancer.
authors: Chang S, Hur JY, Choi YL et al.

title: Self-powered bubble motor microswarms for ultrasensitive detection, monitoring and prediction in cancer liquid biopsies.
authors: Lu H, Qin X, Su C et al.
abstract: Extracellular vesicles (EVs) have shown great potential for disease detection from liquid biopsies. However, the lack of optimized isolation and detection methods limited their clinical application. Here we engineer a bioinspired, reconfigurable, self-powered bubble motor (Butor) microswarm to streamline intelligent isolation and ultrasensitive profiling of circulating EVs for cancer liquid biopsies. Butor microswarm shows jellyfish-like, self-propelled lifting locomotion along lumen-like vertical or inclined tubular path in parallel, allowing rapid isolation (10 min, near 90%) of EV subtypes via three-dimensional directional scanning capture even in high-viscosity biofluids. Furthermore, the buoyancy-activated Butors achieve ultrasensitive EV profiling near a single-particle level, enable early diagnosis of non-small cell lung cancer with an accuracy of up to 94% (95% sensitivity) in a pilot cohort and improve the outcome in cancer staging (I-IV) discrimination, response monitoring of surgical treatment and efficacy prediction of immunotherapy in patients with non-small cell lung cancer. Our self-powered motor represents an intelligent, fast, inexpensive, sensitive and multiplexed liquid biopsy tool for accurate cancer diagnostics and treatment monitoring in clinical settings.

title: Endothelial Activation and Stress Index and Radiation Pneumonitis Risk After Thoracic Radiotherapy in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer.
authors: Xie J, Wei T, Liu X et al.
abstract: Radiation pneumonitis (RP) is a clinically important toxicity after thoracic radiotherapy, and risk assessment should account for treatment dose, systemic therapy, and host response. This retrospective single-center study evaluated whether the endothelial activation and stress index (EASIX) adds predictive information for Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) v5.0 grade ≥2 RP within 6 months after completion of radiotherapy. Clinical, laboratory, treatment, and dosimetric data from 242 patients with non-small cell lung cancer were analyzed. Model A was the clinical-treatment-dosimetric model and included tumor stage, mean lung dose, radiotherapy technique, concurrent chemoradiotherapy, and immune checkpoint inhibitor exposure; Model B was the clinical-treatment-dosimetric model plus EASIX. Discrimination, calibration, repeated stratified 10-fold cross-validation, and 1,000-resample bootstrap validation were assessed. Grade ≥2 RP occurred in 59 patients (grade 2, n=35; grade 3, n=20; grade 4, n=4). Model A achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.826 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.766-0.887), whereas Model B achieved an AUC of 0.903 (95% CI, 0.855-0.951; DeLong p = 0.003). Bootstrap optimism-corrected AUC was 0.886, and the corrected calibration slope was 0.870. The final Youden cutoff was 2.005; EASIX alone had 52.5% sensitivity and therefore should not be used as a standalone test. EASIX may complement established clinical and dosimetric factors for RP risk stratification, but external validation is required.

title: Association Between Myasthenia Gravis and Sarcoidosis: A Case Report.
authors: Amanahou M, Maouelainin ML, Taous A et al.
abstract: Sarcoidosis is a systemic granulomatous disease of unknown cause. Its association with myasthenia gravis has mainly been documented in isolated case reports and small series. We report double-seronegative myasthenia gravis for the antibodies tested, associated with stage I thoracic sarcoidosis and thymic hyperplasia without thymoma. A 46-year-old woman was hospitalized in November 2021 for grade 3 exertional dyspnea according to the modified Medical Research Council scale, associated with fluctuating left-sided ptosis that worsened toward the end of the day. The neostigmine test was positive, with transient improvement in the ptosis. Low-frequency repetitive nerve stimulation demonstrated a decrement compatible with a postsynaptic neuromuscular transmission disorder. Antibodies against the acetylcholine receptor and anti-MuSK antibodies were negative, leading to the diagnosis of double-seronegative myasthenia gravis for the antibodies tested. At the same time, thoracic imaging showed multiple bilateral mediastinal and hilar lymphadenopathies without pulmonary parenchymal involvement. Mediastinoscopy with lymph node biopsy revealed non-necrotizing epithelioid and giant-cell granulomatous lymphadenitis compatible with sarcoidosis. Systemic corticosteroid therapy with prednisone was initiated. The neurological course was marked by worsening myasthenic manifestations, with increased ptosis, diplopia, painful dysphagia, and predominantly left-sided weakness. A course of intravenous immunoglobulin resulted in marked clinical improvement. Thymectomy performed in July 2023 revealed thymic hyperplasia without thymoma. At the latest available follow-up, the patient was asymptomatic and remained under neurological follow-up. The coexistence of sarcoidosis and myasthenia gravis remains rarely described. In this case, the two diagnoses were supported by independent findings. Sarcoidosis was supported by radiological and histological findings, whereas the fluctuating and fatigable nature of the ptosis, the response to neostigmine, and the electrophysiological abnormalities supported the diagnosis of myasthenia gravis. Neurosarcoidosis was the main neurological differential diagnosis. The coexistence of the two diseases may be coincidental and, although an immune-mediated background may be considered, the available data do not demonstrate a specific or causal relationship between sarcoidosis and myasthenia gravis. This case describes a rare association between stage I thoracic sarcoidosis and double-seronegative myasthenia gravis, with thymic hyperplasia without thymoma. It highlights the importance of documenting each condition separately and of investigating a neuromuscular transmission abnormality in the presence of fluctuating ptosis, diplopia, or bulbar involvement in a patient with sarcoidosis, rather than immediately attributing these manifestations to neurosarcoidosis.

authors: Wang S, Zhu J, Jiang J et al.

title: Lung Cancer and Thoracic Malignancies: Staging and Treatment Response.
authors: Kiran MY, Ozkan ZG
journal: Magn Reson Imaging Clin N Am
abstract: This article reviews the clinical role of 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose PET/ computed tomography (CT) in lung cancer and selected thoracic malignancies, focusing on staging and treatment response assessment, while emphasizing major interpretation pitfalls. In lung cancer, emphasis is placed on nodal and metastatic staging, evaluation for recurrence, metabolic response criteria, quantitative PET parameters, and treatment-specific imaging considerations. Selected applications in thymic epithelial tumors and malignant pleural mesothelioma are also discussed. Emerging approaches, including somatostatin receptor PET, fibroblast activation protein inhibitor PET, PET/MR imaging, and artificial intelligence-based PET/CT analysis, are briefly summarized.

title: Tumor-responsive AAV arms cancer cells to enhance CAR-T cell therapy in solid tumors
summary: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T-cell therapy remains limited in solid tumors by the scarcity of suitable target antigens and an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment. Here, we developed a tumor-responsive recombinant adeno-associated virus (rAAV) strategy that harnesses aberrant NF-{kappa}B activity to establish a shared synthetic CAR target across tumor types. Using an NF-{kappa}B-responsive decoy minimal promoter (DMP), rAAV-SA drove tumor-preferential surface expression of a synthetic antigen (SA), enabling antigen-dependent CAR-T-cell activation, degranulation, and cytotoxicity. Systemic rAAV-SA delivery combined with CAR-T cells produced antitumor activity in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) and colorectal cancer xenograft models. We subsequently engineered rAAV-ARMS (antigen redirection and multifunctional secreted effectors), integrating SA expression with tumor-local production of an IL-15/IL-15R sushi-domain fusion, CXCL10, and IFN-{gamma}. Compared with antigen redirection alone, rAAV-ARMS enhanced CAR-T-cell-mediated killing in three-dimensional tumor spheroids and, in a TNBC xenograft model, increased intratumoral T-cell accumulation and improved the efficacy of intravenously administered CAR-T cells, without overt systemic toxicity under the conditions examined. These findings establish a tumor-programmed platform for target-redirected universal CAR-T-cell therapy in solid tumors.
